lesson_scope: Locating and bracketing roots of equations using sign change calculations: defining $f(x) = 0$, evaluating $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, showing $f(a) \cdot f(b) < 0$, and concluding the existence of a root in $(a, b)$ by continuity for polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric equations in radians.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational drill: evaluating a polynomial function at integer endpoints and establishing a sign change.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Standard sign change test evaluating polynomial endpoints to bracket a root.

hints: Define a function $f(x) = x^3 + 2x - 7$. A root of the equation occurs where $f(x) = 0$.
Substitute $x = 1$ and $x = 2$ into $f(x)$ to evaluate $f(1)$ and $f(2)$ separately.
Observe that $f(1) = -4 < 0$ and $f(2) = 5 > 0$. Conclude that since $f(x)$ is continuous and changes sign, a root lies between $1$ and $2$.

walkthrough.text: Define the continuous function $f(x) = x^3 + 2x - 7$.

Evaluate the function at the interval endpoints:
$$f(1) = 1^3 + 2(1) - 7 = 1 + 2 - 7 = -4 < 0$$
$$f(2) = 2^3 + 2(2) - 7 = 8 + 4 - 7 = 5 > 0$$
Since $f(x)$ is a polynomial (and therefore continuous on $[1, 2]$) and changes sign between $x = 1$ and $x = 2$, there exists at least one root in the interval $1 < x < 2$.

ai_rubric.observable: Evaluates $f(1)$ and $f(2)$ for a suitable function $f(x) = x^3 + 2x - 7$ (or equivalent difference).
Obtains correct values $f(1) = -4$ and $f(2) = 5$, notes the change of sign, and concludes that a root lies between $1$ and $2$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured core: differentiation of a quotient involving ln(x) followed by root bracketing of the resulting stationary equation.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Calculus stationary point yielding an equation to be solved numerically.

hints: Recall the quotient rule: $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}$ where $u = \ln x$ and $v = x^2 + 3$.
Compute $u' = \dfrac{1}{x}$ and $v' = 2x$, giving numerator $\dfrac{1}{x}(x^2 + 3) - 2x\ln x$.
At a stationary point, set the numerator equal to $0$: $\dfrac{x^2+3}{x} - 2x\ln x = 0$.
Multiply throughout by $x$ to get $x^2 + 3 - 2x^2 \ln x = 0$, then rearrange to $2x^2 \ln x - x^2 = 3$.

walkthrough.text:
Differentiate $y = \dfrac{\ln x}{x^2 + 3}$ using the quotient rule:
$$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{x}(x^2 + 3) - (\ln x)(2x)}{(x^2 + 3)^2} = \dfrac{\frac{x^2 + 3}{x} - 2x\ln x}{(x^2 + 3)^2}$$

Set $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 0$, which requires the numerator to be zero:
$$\dfrac{x^2 + 3}{x} - 2x\ln x = 0$$

Multiply by $x$:
$$x^2 + 3 - 2x^2 \ln x = 0 \implies 2x^2 \ln x - x^2 = 3$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies quotient rule (or product rule) to differentiate $y = \dfrac{\ln x}{x^2 + 3}$ and sets $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 0$.
Simplifies the numerator $\dfrac{1}{x}(x^2 + 3) - 2x\ln x = 0$ to obtain $2x^2 \ln x - x^2 = 3$ correctly.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Proving root uniqueness via strict monotonicity.

hints: Differentiate $g(x) = 2x + \ln(\cos x) - \ln 2$ with respect to $x$.
Recall that $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\ln(\cos x)) = \dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x} = -\tan x$.
Thus, $g'(x) = 2 - \tan x$.
For $x \in [0, 1]$, the maximum of $\tan x$ is $\tan(1) \approx 1.5574 < 2$, so $g'(x) > 0$ everywhere on $[0, 1]$.
Since $g(x)$ is strictly increasing on $[0, 1]$, it can have at most one root in this interval, proving the root from part (a) is unique.

walkthrough.text:
Differentiate $g(x)$:
$$g'(x) = \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(2x + \ln(\cos x) - \ln 2\right) = 2 + \dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x} = 2 - \tan x$$

Examine the sign of $g'(x)$ on $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$:
Since $\tan x$ is strictly increasing on $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, for $x \in [0, 1]$ we have $0 \leqslant \tan x \leqslant \tan(1) \approx 1.5574 < 2$.

Therefore, $g'(x) = 2 - \tan x > 0$ for all $x \in [0, 1]$. Because $g(x)$ is strictly increasing, it is a one-to-one function on $[0, 1]$ and can cross the $x$-axis at most once. Hence, the root in $(0.3, 0.4)$ is the unique root in $[0, 1]$.

ai_rubric.observable: Differentiates $g(x) = 2x + \ln(\cos x) - \ln 2$ to obtain $g'(x) = 2 - \tan x$.
States that $\tan x < 2$ for $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$, so $g'(x) > 0$ (strictly increasing), which proves the root in $[0, 1]$ is unique.

hints: Set up the integral for the area under the curve: $\text{Area} = \int_0^p \dfrac{1}{2x + 1}\,\text{d}x$.
Use the standard result $\int \dfrac{1}{ax+b}\,\text{d}x = \dfrac{1}{a}\ln|ax+b|$ to integrate.
Evaluate $\left[\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2x+1)\right]_0^p = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2p+1) - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(1) = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2p+1)$.
Set the area equal to the rectangle area $0.4p$, giving $\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2p+1) = 0.4p \implies \ln(2p+1) = 0.8p$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the area under the curve from $x = 0$ to $x = p$:
$$\int_0^p \dfrac{1}{2x + 1}\,\text{d}x = \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2x + 1) \right]_0^p = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2p + 1) - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(1) = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2p + 1)$$
The area of the rectangle is $\text{width} \times \text{height} = p \times 0.4 = 0.4p$.

Equate the two areas:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(2p + 1) = 0.4p \implies \ln(2p + 1) = 0.8p$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard capstone: subtle domain discontinuity analysis combined with numerical root isolation for a rational-exponential equation.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Domain restriction and numerical verification under algebraic simplification.

hints: For part (i), substitute $x = 2.1$ and $x = 2.2$ into $h(x) = x - \text{e}^{-x} - 2$.
For part (ii), observe that the original left-hand side $\dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$ has $x - 2$ in the denominator, so $x = 2$ is outside the natural domain (point discontinuity).

Explain that for any value $x \neq 2$, the algebraic identity $\dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2} = \dfrac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} = x + 2$ holds exactly. Because the root $\alpha \in (2.1, 2.2)$ is strictly greater than $2$, it is a genuine root of the original equation.

walkthrough.text: Since $h(x)$ is continuous on $[2.1, 2.2]$ and changes sign, a root of $h(x) = 0$ lies in $2.1 < x < 2.2$.

Examine the original equation domain:
The expression $\dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$ requires $x \neq 2$ to avoid division by zero. Thus $x = 2$ is an excluded point (a hole / removable discontinuity) where the equation is undefined.

However, for all $x \neq 2$, $\dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2} = x + 2$ is strictly valid. Since the root lies in $(2.1, 2.2)$, we have $x > 2$, which satisfies the domain restriction $x \neq 2$. Therefore, the root is a completely valid solution to the original equation.

ai_rubric.observable: Evaluates $h(2.1) \approx -0.0225$ and $h(2.2) \approx 0.0892$ to show a change of sign.
Notes that $h(2.1) < 0$ and $h(2.2) > 0$, confirming a root of $h(x) = 0$ in $(2.1, 2.2)$.

Explains that although the original equation is undefined at the point discontinuity $x = 2$, the root $\alpha \in (2.1, 2.2)$ satisfies $x \neq 2$ where the simplification $\dfrac{x^2-4}{x-2} = x+2$ is algebraically exact and valid.
